body.objective: Students will be able to create a relief or monoprint.
body.iCan: I can create a relief or monoprint.
successCriteria: I can design an image for relief printing in reverse
I can carve or prepare a plate safely
I can pull a consistent edition and label it correctly
body.hook: Before the printing press, every image had to be made by hand, one at a time. Printmaking changed that: carve a block once and you can pull dozens of prints. Artists from Japanese ukiyo-e masters to Inuit printmakers in Kinngait (Cape Dorset) have used it to share images with the world.

A one-of-a-kind print made from a painted or inked smooth plate.
A small roller used to spread ink evenly.
A set of identical prints from the same plate.
Lining up the paper and plate so each print is in the same place.

study.title: Carve, Ink, Print
study.question: How does printmaking change the way an artist designs an image?
study.passage:
Materials: soft-cut lino or foam blocks, lino cutters with guards, bench hooks, water-based block ink, brayers, inking plates, wooden spoons or a press, paper.
Safety: Always carve away from your body with the block held in a bench hook. Keep your free hand behind the blade.
Part 1, Design (15 minutes): Draw a design the size of the block. Use strong contrast: large black and white shapes. Remember that the print will be reversed, so text must be written backward. Shade areas you will NOT carve.
Part 2, Transfer and carve (30 minutes): Transfer the design by rubbing a pencil drawing face-down onto the block. Carve the white areas away using a V-gouge for lines and a U-gouge for clearing.
Part 3, Ink and print (20 minutes): Roll a thin, even layer of ink on the plate until it sounds like velvet. Ink the block, place the paper using a registration jig and burnish with a spoon. Pull a proof.
Part 4, Edition (15 minutes): Make adjustments, then pull an edition of three to five. Sign in pencil below the image: edition number (for example 2/5), title, signature, year.
Monoprint option: Paint directly onto a smooth plexiglass plate and print once.
study.source: Original studio task written for this lesson; printmaking conventions summarized from standard art education sources.

study.product: Produce a signed edition of three relief prints (or a series of monoprints) and write a short reflection on how the process shaped your image.

examples.title: Reversal
examples.problem: You want the word "ART" to read correctly. How do you carve it?
steps: The print is a mirror image
examples.answer: Carve it backward on the block
examples.explore: What other parts of an image would flip?

examples.title: Positive space
examples.problem: Which areas print in a relief print?
examples.answer: The areas you did not carve
examples.explore: What colour are the carved areas on the print?

examples.title: Edition label
examples.problem: Label the third print of an edition of eight.

examples.title: Troubleshooting
examples.problem: A print is blotchy with gaps. What went wrong?
examples.answer: Re-roll ink evenly and burnish more firmly
examples.explore: How would too much ink look?

practice.q: Why must text be carved backward?
practice.a: The print is a mirror image of the block.

practice.q: Which gouge is best for clearing large areas?
What does 4/10 mean on a print?
practice.a: The fourth print in an edition of ten.
Lining up paper and block so each print matches.

practice.q: How do you know ink is rolled correctly?
practice.a: It is thin and even and sounds velvety.

practice.q: Why use strong contrast in a relief design?
practice.a: Fine grey tones are hard to carve; bold shapes print clearly.
Relief makes repeatable editions; monoprints are unique.

practice.q: How did printmaking help Inuit artists in Kinngait?
practice.a: It let them make editions of their drawings to share and sell widely.

practice.q: A print has smudged edges. Suggest two fixes.
practice.a: Clean the block edges, use a registration jig, avoid sliding the paper.

practice.q: Why might an artist choose printmaking for a political message?
practice.a: Many copies can be made and shared quickly and cheaply.

misconceptions: Thinking more ink makes a better print
Thinking prints in an edition are copies, not original artworks

items.answer: B) printmaking

A brayer.

items.q: Describe how to sign a print.
items.answer: In pencil below the image: number/total, title, signature, year.

items.q: Give one safety rule for carving.
items.answer: Cut away from your body using a bench hook.

items.q: What is the difference between positive and negative space in a relief print?
items.answer: Positive is the raised inked area; negative is the carved area that stays paper-coloured.
Relief is carved and repeatable; monoprint is painted and unique.

items.q: Explain why printmaking has been important for sharing art and ideas.
items.answer: It makes many copies cheaply, so images and messages reach more people.
